title: Benizara and Kakezara: The Crimson Dish and the Broken Bowl (Japan)

full_text:
In an ancient mountain province of Japan lived a widower who had a daughter named Benizara (Crimson Dish), whose mother had left her a small crimson porcelain saucer.
The father remarried a harsh woman with a daughter named Kakezara (Broken Dish).
The stepmother favored Kakezara, loading Benizara with all household drudgery: carrying water from mountain gorges, cutting bamboo, and gathering wild chestnuts in the snow.

One autumn, the stepmother gave each girl a woven bamboo basket, promising a fine silk kimono to whoever filled her basket with chestnuts first.
To Kakezara she gave a tight, strong basket; to Benizara she gave a basket with a hole in the bottom!

Benizara worked in the mountain woods, but every chestnut slipped through the hole onto the moss.
Weeping, she followed the trail of fallen nuts to a solitary mountain hut, where lived an ancient mountain woman.
Benizara bowed politely, swept the hut's hearth, prepared tea, and washed the old woman’s rice bowl.
The mountain woman smiled:
'Gentle maiden, take this woven rush basket that never empties, and take this magic box. When thou art in need, tap the lid.'

Benizara returned home with her basket overflowing with sweet chestnuts.
The envious stepmother gave Kakezara a new kimono, but left Benizara in her hemp rags.

When the young Lord of the Province traveled through their village on his ceremonial hunt, the villagers gathered to welcome him.
The stepmother locked Benizara in the rice cellar and took Kakezara to the festival.
Benizara tapped the magic box.
Instantly, her hemp rags turned into a layered silk kimono dyed the color of autumn maple leaves, with a sash of gold brocade and wooden geta clogs lacquered in vermilion!

She stood beneath a blossoming cherry tree as the Lord passed.
The Lord halted his retinue, enchanted by her graceful demeanor.
To test her mind, the Lord composed the first half of a classical waka poem:
'Upon the mountain path the autumn leaves fall deep...'
Benizara bowed modestly, completing the poem with flawless classical meter:
'Yet through the scarlet boughs the moon of virtue shines!'

The Lord was astonished by her profound learning and refined spirit.
When the stepmother pushed Kakezara forward, Kakezara spoke only crude, greedy words, humiliating her mother.
The Lord chose Benizara as his bride, escorting her to his castle with full samurai honor, celebrating her as a lady whose gentle conduct reflected the pure beauty of the mountain snow.
moral: Gentle humility, filial respect, and poetic refinement blossom into noble honor, while harshness shatters like clay.
